audience.programmeDescription: Delft’s Computer Science and Engineering bachelor combines programming and software engineering with computer systems, algorithms, mathematics and AI. Practical work and projects develop the analysis, design and evaluation of digital systems.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR programme combines substantial programming, software, databases, networks, algorithms and mathematical methods with machine learning and responsible AI. It offers related computing study, with important differences in specialist coverage and compulsory project work.

curriculum.limitation: The two language tracks have the same academic structure. The bilingual track includes Dutch and English teaching and assessment. Five electives are selected from the adopted list; later annual offerings may change. Zero-credit mentoring is also compulsory.

componentNotes.CSE200: Compulsory 15-EC team software project for a client. For 2026 entrants, Programming, HCI and AI-Assisted Prototyping, Software Design and Engineering, and the Collaborative Development Project must be passed first.
componentNotes.CSE300: Compulsory individual 15-EC supervised computer-science research project and scientific article. For students entering in 2026, access follows the programme’s enrolment and project-registration rules.
componentNotes.cse-minor: Approved 30-EC minor, normally a thematic programme, subject to overlap and entry rules. Study abroad has additional progression and approval conditions.

cellNotes.text: Computational image analysis and recognition, rather than computer graphics or rendering.
Experimental design and multivariable analysis using health and behavioural examples; a software or user-interface project is not guaranteed.

concept: A computing programme centred on programming, software development, databases, networks and operating systems, algorithms, discrete mathematics, probability and numerical methods. Machine learning, computer vision, neural networks, optimisation and reinforcement learning provide substantial intelligent-systems study. Empirical research and multivariable statistics support evaluation; ethical reasoning and the economic and regulatory study of AI examine responsible engineering. It does not reproduce Delft’s computer-hardware organisation, technical security, dedicated human-computer interaction and graphics, specialist electives or compulsory large software and individual research projects.
finding: The core is substantial computing, not a business/communication programme with an AI label. Human-centred interaction/graphics and technical security gaps remain explicit; visual recognition and introductory data work are not relabelled. Bilingual language requirements and compulsory zero-credit mentoring are visible. Reader text contains no API/provenance investigation; old-cohort interpretation stays internal. No technical-project topic, master-admission or professional entitlement promised.
runtimeScope: No R/Shiny/browser software installed/launched, screenshots or live modals. Shared app/renderer code unchanged. Representative actual rendering remains a separate final-release gate.
